stemMd:
Historians of technology have long been drawn to the **(i)** ______ inventor, the solitary figure whose flash of insight remakes an industry. Recent archival work on the early refrigeration trade suggests that such accounts are **(ii)** ______: the crucial patents were filed within months of one another by half a dozen engineers in three countries, none of whom knew of the others' work. What looks like genius may be nothing more than the moment at which a problem becomes **(iii)** ______ — the moment when materials, capital and demand have converged to put a solution within reach of anyone who happens to be looking.

**Blank (i):** prosaic / heroic / derivative

**Blank (ii):** misleading / exhaustive / indispensable

**Blank (iii):** obsolete / fashionable / tractable
instructionsMd: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices. All blanks must be correct; there is no credit for a partially correct answer.
explanationMd:
A three-blank item rewards solving the blanks in the order the evidence allows, not in the order they appear.

**Blank (i) — the easiest, because it is defined in apposition.** The phrase immediately after the comma renames the inventor: **"the solitary figure whose flash of insight remakes an industry."** That is a description of grandeur and singular achievement. **"Heroic"** matches it.

**Blank (ii) — fixed by the colon.** The colon introduces the evidence, and the evidence cuts against the picture just drawn: half a dozen engineers in three countries reached the same invention independently and almost simultaneously. If many people arrive at a result at once, no single figure's insight explains it, so the heroic accounts give a false picture. **"Misleading"** is that judgement.

**Blank (iii) — fixed by the dash.** The clause after the dash defines the blank: materials, capital and demand have converged **"to put a solution within reach of anyone who happens to be looking."** A problem in that condition is one that can now be solved by ordinary effort. **"Tractable"** means exactly manageable or amenable to solution.

**The answer is heroic, misleading and tractable.**

**How to check.** Read the completed passage straight through and confirm it makes one argument rather than three unrelated assertions. It does: historians admire the heroic inventor; the simultaneity evidence shows that admiration to be misleading; and the explanation offered is that invention arrives when a problem turns tractable. If a chosen word leaves any sentence merely acceptable rather than load-bearing in that chain, re-open it. Since all three blanks must be right for any credit, the efficient order is to lock the blank with an explicit gloss first and use the argument it establishes to constrain the others.

distractorRationale.blank1-a: "Prosaic" means dull and ordinary. It is the opposite of the appositive gloss, which describes a solitary figure whose flash of insight remakes an industry, and historians would not be "drawn to" a figure they found dull.
distractorRationale.blank1-c: "Derivative" means unoriginal. That is not the picture historians were drawn to, and it flatly contradicts "flash of insight" in the same sentence.
distractorRationale.blank2-b: "Exhaustive" means thorough and complete. Thoroughness is not what simultaneous independent patents call into question; the evidence attacks the accuracy of the heroic story, not its level of detail.
distractorRationale.blank2-c: "Indispensable" means necessary. It reverses the argument: the passage uses the archival evidence to undercut the heroic account rather than to establish that historians cannot do without it.
distractorRationale.blank3-a: "Obsolete" means outdated and no longer in use. A problem that has just attracted six independent solutions is newly live, not superseded, and the clause after the dash describes a solution coming within reach rather than a problem going away.
distractorRationale.blank3-b: "Fashionable" means currently popular. The word is tempting because "demand" appears in the same clause, but the clause defines the blank as a solution being within reach of anyone looking, which is a statement about feasibility rather than about popularity.

independentSolve.workingNotes: Blank (i) is glossed by "the solitary figure whose flash of insight remakes an industry", so heroic (blank1-b); prosaic and derivative contradict that. Simultaneous independent patents undercut the lone-genius story, so the accounts are misleading (blank2-a), not exhaustive or indispensable. Blank (iii) is glossed as the moment a solution comes "within reach", i.e. tractable (blank3-c); obsolete is the opposite and fashionable ignores the within-reach gloss.

review.notes: Author solved as heroic / misleading / tractable. Blank (i) is glossed by the appositive 'the solitary figure whose flash of insight remakes an industry'; blank (ii) by the colon evidence of six simultaneous independent patents; blank (iii) by the post-dash clause about a solution coming within reach of anyone looking. Each of the six wrong words was tested against its own gloss.
